title: Samarkand: Jewel of the Silk Road

cards.h: A city that sat at the crossroads
cards.b:
Samarkand, in today's Uzbekistan, is one of the oldest cities on the Silk Road. Its name is still a byword for the caravan trade between China, India, Persia and Rome.

The city shows how trade, faith, science and war mixed together over two thousand years. Each empire that ruled it left something behind.

Alexander the Great took the city, then called Maracanda, in 329 BCE. Its people were Sogdians, a Persian-speaking trading people whose merchants spread across Central Asia and China.

Sogdian merchants ran the trade in silk and other goods. In 1907 explorers found ancient Sogdian letters near Dunhuang, written around 313 CE. They describe famine and hardship in China, which shows how news travelled along the route.

In 751 an Abbasid army met a Chinese Tang force at the Talas river in Central Asia. The Abbasids won. Among the prisoners were Chinese craftsmen who knew how to make paper.

Paper making spread west from Samarkand, and then into the Islamic world. It helped make books cheaper and spread learning across the Middle East and later Europe.

Ruy González de Clavijo (embassy in 1404)

A Spanish envoy sent by the king of Castile, Clavijo visited the court of Timur in Samarkand. He wrote a detailed account of the city, its gardens, its feasts and its markets.

His book is one of the best European eyewitness accounts of Central Asia in the 1400s.
Samarkand changed hands many times. Its wealth came from its location, and its prestige came from the empires that built in it.

Timur, known in English as Tamerlane, made Samarkand his capital from 1370. He used war loot and captured craftsmen to build mosques, palaces and gardens. The Bibi-Khanym mosque was among the greatest buildings of its day.

Timur's empire stretched from Anatolia to India. His court was a place of splendour, and his conquests were brutal. Both facts sit side by side in the city's history.

cards.h: Was the Silk Road a single highway?
cards.b:
The phrase "Silk Road" suggests one road with caravans going from China to Rome. It is a convenient picture, and it appears in many books and films.

Historians argue it was a network of routes, by land and sea, linked by many merchants. Very little silk went all the way from China to Rome. Ideas, religions, diseases and goods moved in short hops from city to city.

Ulugh Beg, a grandson of Timur, was a ruler and a scientist. He built a great observatory in Samarkand around 1420 and produced a star catalogue with around a thousand stars. His madrasa stands on the Registan square.

His reign ended in violence in 1449, when his own son had him killed. His astronomy lived on, and his star catalogue was copied for generations.

The Registan is a square in the centre of the city with three great madrasas: Ulugh Beg's, Sher-Dor and Tilla-Kari. Their blue tiled facades are some of the most famous images of Central Asia.

The word Registan means "sandy place". The square was once the heart of trade and public life. Today it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a symbol of Uzbekistan.

cards.h: Did the Silk Road spread plague?
cards.b:
The Black Death of the 1340s is linked by some historians to trade routes that ran through Central Asia. Plague bacteria may have moved with caravans and ships, though the exact path is debated.

Other historians doubt that trade routes were the main cause. The debate shows how hard it is to trace a disease to its first path, and how much we still rely on guesses from texts and graves.

In December 1398 Timur's army sacked Delhi. Timur took vast loot and captured craftsmen, including masons and artists, and carried them back to Samarkand to build his new city.

The Delhi Sultanate was weak at the time, and the sack was a shock. Indian craftsmen helped shape the architecture of Samarkand, and the city's buildings carry the memory of that exchange.

Five things to remember
  1. Alexander took Maracanda in 329 BCE.
  2. The battle of Talas in 751 spread papermaking west.
  3. Timur made Samarkand his capital from 1370.
  4. Ulugh Beg built a famous observatory around 1420.
  5. The Silk Road was a network, not a single highway.
Think about it
  • How did conquest and science live side by side in Samarkand?
  • Who really moved goods along the Silk Road?
